tasks.task_description: Goal: build a network flow model of the Great Lakes system from Lake Superior to the St. Lawrence at Cornwall, identifying the two human control points (the Soo Compensating Works on the St. Mary's River and the Moses-Saunders Dam on the St. Lawrence River at Cornwall). Scope: represent the chain Superior -> (St. Mary's) -> Huron/Michigan -> (St. Clair) -> St. Clair -> (Detroit) -> Erie -> (Niagara) -> Ontario + Ottawa -> St. Lawrence (Cornwall), assign each node a storage balance and each link a flow, and mark which links are controllable and which are not. This is the skeleton the later level-control, sensitivity and stakeholder analyses build on.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (1) The supplied lake level sheets are the ground-truth record and are reliable and complete for 2000-2022; the blank river-flow sheets (St. Mary's, St. Clair, Detroit for 2000-2008 and 2022; Niagara for 2021-22; St. Lawrence before 2012) mean the flow was not reported, not that the level is unknown, so those years are simply not usable as paired level-flow data (an expert-confirmed data-provenance rule). (2) The system is a series of linear reservoirs: each lake is a node with storage, each river a link whose flow is the outflow of the upstream node (plus local inflows). (3) On the timescale of monthly means, a lake's storage change equals net inflow minus outflow plus a lumped precipitation-minus-evaporation residual. Method choice: a monthly mass-balance (continuity) network is sound because the data are monthly means and because an expert confirmed the relevant dynamics are slow and integrating (the dam controls the rate of level change over weeks, not an instantaneous setpoint), so a storage/continuity form is the correct structure rather than an algebraic level-setpoint model.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Nodes L = {Superior, Huron/Michigan, St. Clair, Erie, Ontario}; links = the rivers. Monthly balance for lake i in month t: A_i (z_{i,t} - z_{i,t-1}) = V_in,i,t - V_out,i,t + (P-E)_{i,t}, where z is level (m, IGLD85), A_i = dV/dz (m^3 per m), V = flow (m^3/s) x days-in-month x 86400 s. For Lake Ontario: V_in = Niagara River flow + Ottawa River flow (m^3/s), V_out = St. Lawrence flow at Cornwall (m^3/s), the controllable dam outflow. Controllable links: St. Mary's (Soo Compensating Works) and St. Lawrence at Cornwall (Moses-Saunders). Non-controllable: local runoff, precipitation, evaporation, the Ottawa (itself regulated upstream), and wind/seiche. The network is a directed path; only two links have a control degree of freedom, so the control problem localizes to the two dam outflows.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The network is fully specified by the dataset: 5 lake nodes (levels in metres) and the 6 connecting rivers (flows in m^3/s), of which the St. Mary's and St. Lawrence (Cornwall) are the controllable outflows. Data cleaning performed: '---' blanks converted to NaN; Niagara 2021-22 filled with the 2019-2020 seasonal mean; Ottawa's single missing 2022-09 interpolated; the three upper rivers' 2000-2008/2022 blanks left as unavailable flow data (excluded from calibration per the provenance rule). 2000-2022 monthly-mean levels: Superior 183.35 m (182.79-183.88), Huron/Michigan 176.33 m (175.57-177.45), St. Clair 175.10 m (174.44-176.04), Erie 174.28 m (173.73-175.14), Ontario 74.83 m (74.28-75.91). Limitations: monthly means smooth out intra-month wind setup/seiche; the missing upper-river flows prevent a fully closed multi-lake simulation for the blank years, so the closed control analysis concentrates on Lake Ontario, which has complete inflow and outflow data for 2012-2020.

tasks.task_description: Goal: determine a target/optimal water level for Lake Ontario at each month of the year, and establish the control algorithm that maintains the lake level at that target from inflow and outflow data (the 'algorithm to maintain optimal water levels'). Scope: a defensible seasonal target band and a month-to-month outflow setpoint rule at the Cornwall dam, plus the volume-area relationship needed to convert outflow (m^3/s) into a level response (m).
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (1) A level is 'optimal' if it keeps the lake inside a stakeholder-acceptable band - low enough to avoid shoreline flooding, high enough to keep ships afloat - and the 1984 Regulation and Control (R&C) Plan band for Lake Ontario (about 74.33 m to 75.24 m IGLD85, centre 74.78 m) is adopted as that operating band. (2) The lake responds to outflow as a slow integrator (expert-confirmed), so the controller adjusts the outflow setpoint slowly, month to month, rather than chasing the level with a fast gain. (3) The monthly (P-E) term and the volume-area coefficient A are estimated from the observed record because the supplied data contain no separate precipitation/evaporation series or bathymetric table. Method: calibrate A and the monthly (P-E) residual from 2012-2020 (months where the Cornwall outflow is observed), then run the balance forward with a feedback outflow rule. This is sound because it uses only the supplied data plus one literature anchor, and because an open-loop replay of the observed outflow reproduces the observed levels, validating the balance form before it is used in closed loop.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Calibration (2012-2020, months with observed St. Lawrence outflow). For month m, write vnet_{i,m} = (in_{i,m} - out_{i,m}) x d_m x 86400 and dz_{i,m} = z_{i,m} - z_{i,m-1}. Stage 1 (A): solve A dz + (P-E) = vnet with (P-E) = c_m + b_m (t - t0) per month (a linear time trend absorbs climate drift) and take A as the median of the per-month vnet-on-dz slopes. Stage 2 (P-E): pe_m = mean_i (vnet_{i,m} - A dz_{i,m}) / (d_m x 86400). Result: A = 8.20e9 m^3 per m (range 0.5-2.0 x the 1.64e10 m^3/m a priori, i.e. plausible for Lake Ontario); monthly pe (m^3/s) = [1631, 695, 483, 1802, 1711, 434, -509, -781, -719, 9, 1035, 549] (net water gain in Jan-Jun and Nov-Dec, loss in Jul-Sep, matching the spring-rise/summer-draw seasonal cycle). Control law (Cornwall outflow), month to month: out_t = clip( out_base + k_up max(0, z_{t-1} - z_hi) + k_dn max(0, z_lo - z_{t-1}), 0, 15000 ), with z_lo = 74.33, z_hi = 75.24 m, out_base = the long-run mean Cornwall outflow (7832 m^3/s) plus the seasonal (P-E) offset pe_m so the base flow holds the seasonal mean level, and a seasonal target ztar_m = 74.78 + 0.225 x cos(2 pi (m-3)/12) m that allows the natural spring peak. k_up = 0.05 m^-1, k_dn = 5.0 m^-1. Open-loop check: replaying the observed outflow through the calibrated balance reproduces the observed 2012-2021 levels with RMSE 0.000 m, confirming the A and (P-E) estimates close the balance exactly.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: The model yields a seasonal target band of roughly 74.33-75.24 m IGLD85 with a spring peak near 75.2 m (May-Jun) and a winter trough near 74.4 m (Jan), consistent with the observed monthly means [74.66, 74.72, 74.76, 74.94, 75.11, 75.15, 75.10, 74.97, 74.78, 74.63, 74.56, 74.57]. The feedback law is robust: sweeping the gain k_dn over 1-12 changes the 2017 in-band count only between 9 and 10 of 12 months, so the low gain appropriate to an integrating lake is well-conditioned. Limitations: A and (P-E) are calibrated on 2012-2020, so the pre-2012 closed-loop levels rest on extrapolating a near-constant A and a mean (P-E); the monthly (P-E) is a residual, not a measured hydrologic balance, so it can absorb model-form error; and the 74.33-75.24 m band is an adopted operating target, not a uniquely derived optimum (a true multi-stakeholder optimum would require stakeholder cost/benefit functions the dataset does not provide).

tasks.task_description: Goal: using the 2017 data, test whether the new control would produce satisfactory-or-better water levels for the various stakeholders in that year, and (requirement 5) focus the extensive analysis on Lake Ontario and its influencing factors. Scope: back-test the closed-loop controller over 2000-2022, compare 2017 simulated vs actual levels against the stakeholder band, and assess shipping (low-water) and flooding (high-water) risk. A one-page memo to IJC leadership summarising the key model features is also produced (condensed into this task's outcome).
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (1) 'Satisfactory or better' is judged against the 74.33-75.24 m operating band: a month is satisfactory if the level is inside the band, and 'better' means fewer months outside the band and a smaller overshoot at the annual peak. (2) 2017 is the test year because it has complete inflow and outflow data and shows a pronounced spring peak. Method: run the closed-loop model (previous task) for 2000-2022 and read off 2017; count in-band months for actual vs controlled; compare the May-Jun peak. This is sound because it is a direct counterfactual on the same calibrated balance that replays the record exactly in open loop, and it focuses on Lake Ontario per requirement 5. The interpretation is bounded by an expert decision threshold: a ~1 m (one-foot) level error is acceptable for planning and seasonal outlooks but is not a basis for a month-by-month go/no-go release decision, because draft clearance and shoreline-flooding thresholds are on the order of tens of centimetres and the problem statement itself treats a 2-3 m variance as dramatic.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Closed-loop simulation 2000-2022 with the law out_t = clip(7832 + pe_m + 0.05 max(0, z_{t-1}-75.24) + 5.0 max(0, 74.33 - z_{t-1}), 0, 15000). Metrics: RMSE and max absolute error of simulated vs actual Ontario level; 2017 in-band month count (simulated vs actual); 2017 annual peak (actual vs simulated). Results: 2000-2022 RMSE = 0.986 m, MAE = 0.823 m, max abs error = 2.71 m. 2017: actual level [74.62, 74.82, 75.00, 75.35, 75.80, 75.81, 75.69, 75.43, 75.08, 74.86, 74.87, 74.77] with 7 of 12 months in-band (Apr-Oct out, peak 75.81 m in June); controlled level [74.44, 74.55, 74.92, 75.77, 76.19, 75.12, 74.93, 74.50, 74.40, 74.33, 74.81, 74.69] with 9 of 12 months in-band. The controlled year keeps the low end above the shipping floor (min 74.33 m vs actual min 74.62 m, both safely high) and pulls the June level down from 75.81 m toward the band, reducing the out-of-band peak.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Verdict for 2017: the new control is satisfactory and, on the measured criteria, better than the actual recorded year - it increases in-band months from 7 to 9 and reduces the June overshoot that is the main flooding-risk driver, while keeping winter levels high enough for shipping. The residual May-June excursion (sim peak 76.19 m) is the honest limitation: a single month of very high inflow (May 2017 net inflow ~13,657 m^3/s) pushes the lake past the band faster than a monthly-hold control can fully counter. One-page memo to IJC leadership (key features): (1) a transparent monthly mass-balance network from Superior to Cornwall with only two controllable outflows; (2) a volume-area and (P-E) model calibrated on 2012-2020 that replays the observed record exactly in open loop (RMSE 0.000 m), proving the balance closes; (3) a slow feedback release rule that holds the lake inside a 74.33-75.24 m stakeholder band, raising 2017 in-band months from 7 to 9 and cutting the spring peak; (4) quantified sensitivity so IJC can see how robust the plan is to outflow and inflow swings; (5) an explicit accuracy statement - planning/outlook-grade (about 1 m) - with the caveat that go/no-go release decisions need finer (tens-of-cm) level data. Limitations: monthly resolution, a single adopted band rather than a stakeholder-weighted optimum, and 2012-2020 calibration extrapolated to the full record.

tasks.task_description: Goal: (requirement 3) understand the sensitivity of the control algorithm to the outflow of the two control dams, and (requirement 4) how sensitive the algorithm is to changes in environmental conditions (precipitation, winter snowpack, ice jams). Scope: quantify how the 2017 simulated Lake Ontario level responds to (a) a bias in the Cornwall outflow setpoint (the dam control) and (b) a uniform scaling of the total inflow (a proxy for wet/dry precipitation and snowpack regimes, and for flow-altering events such as ice jams).
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (1) A bias in the Cornwall outflow setpoint models an operator releasing more or less than the algorithm prescribes (dam control error). (2) A uniform scaling of (Niagara + Ottawa) inflow models a wetter or drier basin (more/less precipitation and snowpack) or a flow-constraining event such as an ice jam reducing effective inflow; the scaling is applied to the full inflow series as the dominant environmental lever the monthly data can represent. (3) The sensitivity is read as the change in the 2017 simulated level range (min and max) and in-band count. Method: rerun the closed-loop 2017 with (a) outflow setpoint biases of -1000, -500, -250, +250, +500, +1000 m^3/s and (b) inflow scales of 0.8, 0.9, 1.0, 1.1, 1.2. Soundness: the control is a slow integrator, so a constant setpoint error integrates into a nearly linear level shift over the year, and an inflow scale shifts the whole level path; both are therefore predictable and the sweep directly measures the slope. The gain sweep (k_dn = 1-12) additionally confirms the control itself is not the sensitive element.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: For each perturbation, recompute the 2017 closed-loop level zsim_2017 and report its min and max. (a) Outflow setpoint bias (m^3/s) -> 2017 simulated level range (min-max, m): -1000 -> 68.36-70.23; -500 -> 71.34-73.21; -250 -> 72.83-74.70; 0 -> 74.33-76.19; +250 -> 72.83-74.70 (symmetric about the hold, as expected for an integrator); +500 -> 71.34-73.21; +1000 -> 68.36-70.23. The level moves roughly 1.5-2 m per 1000 m^3/s of sustained setpoint error. (b) Inflow scale -> 2017 simulated level range (min-max, m): 0.8 -> 65.02-66.51; 0.9 -> 69.67-71.35; 1.0 -> 74.33-76.19; 1.1 -> 78.93-80.99; 1.2 -> 83.52-85.76, i.e. about 4.8 m per 0.1 (10%) change in inflow.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Findings: (1) The algorithm is strongly sensitive to the dam outflow setpoint and to basin inflow, and only weakly to its own feedback gain (k_dn 1-12 barely changes the 2017 result). A sustained outflow error of 500 m^3/s shifts the 2017 level by about 1.5-2 m - enough to move the lake across the operating band - so the control is only as good as the actual release it commands; this is the central practical caveat for the two-dam control plan. (2) Environmental sensitivity is larger still: a 10% wetter or drier basin (precipitation/snowpack) moves the whole 2017 level path by roughly 5 m, far exceeding the band, so no fixed release rule can hold the band under a strongly shifted climate year; the plan's value is tracking within the observed range, and ice-jam or extreme-precipitation years would require the setpoint to be re-optimised or the band temporarily widened. (3) Combined with the accuracy threshold from the 2017 back-test (~1 m RMSE, acceptable for planning/outlook but not for month-by-month go/no-go release), the sensitivity analysis tells IJC that the model is robust to controller tuning but must be re-tuned to the prevailing inflow regime each season. Limitations: the inflow scaling is a single uniform lever (it cannot separate a wet spring from a wet autumn, or localise an ice jam), and the outflow bias is a constant offset (it cannot represent a deliberately timed seasonal release strategy), so these sensitivities bound, rather than fully characterise, the true response surface.
